title: About Structures and Systems - Intro
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Martin Skelton introduces structures and systems as the fourth factor that affects learning, arguing that these unglamorous background mechanisms shape outcomes far more than people notice. He contrasts two good customer experiences (overnight delivery, a proactive refund) with two poor ones (a website showing backstage stock, the strained NHS) to show how systems determine whether an organisation serves people well. He then turns to the sheer complexity of school life, from timetables and marking to recruitment, safeguarding and governance, each held together by systems that are either fit for purpose or not. Good schools get consistency and positive culture from them, while weak ones waste time and energy. His central point is that learning, as the school's Hedgehog Concept, should be the test for every system, and he ends with questions inviting readers to audit their own.
points: Skelton argues that background systems largely decide whether experiences are good or bad, using customer-service and NHS examples to show it is true of every organisation.
The stock-count anecdote shows a system designed for the organisation's convenience rather than for the person it serves, a test schools can apply to their own processes.
He maps how much of a school day depends on coordinated systems, from room moves and resources to marking, recording and parent information.
Good systems must pass a positive-purpose, easy-to-administer and widely-consented test, otherwise they cause havoc and drain energy.
The closing challenge is to watch which systems break most often and whether they are ever reviewed specifically with learning in mind.
quotes: The reality is that systems, structures and processes that run in the background, have a huge impact on whether outcomes are going to be good or bad, positive or negative. There is hardly a moment in our lives where our pleasure or displeasure, satisfaction or dissatisfaction isn’t the result of the good or bad contribution of some systems, structures and processes.

Both were display models and I couldn’t buy either. The website wasn’t showing buyable stock for the customer’s benefit; it was simply regurgitating the shop’s backstage stock count, developed for themselves.

Systems, structures and processes are, except to a minority of people, at the less sexy end of almost all organisations. I don’t think much about how my shoes are made but I do think a lot about what they look like and how long they last.

Each of these aspects of school life is individually hung together by systems, structures and process that are either good and fit for purpose or not. Each of them is successfully or unsuccessfully joined with another set of fit-for-purpose - or not -systems, structures and processes.

As in all organisations, these systems and structures have the capacity to be helpful if they can pass the positive purpose, easy to administer and consented to by most people test. In really good schools, the systems and structures are super helpful, support effective consistency of action and contribute much to a positive culture. In not so good schools and not so good organisations, they cause havoc, suck energy and waste time.

And so to learning. In the context of a life of a school across a year, learning has to take its place as one of many things that are supported, or not, by different systems. structures and processes. But, as the hedgehog concept of the school, as the very simple idea that learning is the frame of reference for all their decisions, learning should occupy the central place as we think about how systems, structures and processes impact on what is happening and how students are benefiting from the combined efforts of the community that is trying to help them get better.

How much time do you spend reviewing your systems and structures specifically with learning in mind? Does the frequency with which you do this suggest that learning really is the simple central idea that affects all your decisions?
